runs.text: i, que tem bom olho no julgar das couſas.

lines.note: This continues Meqiqi from f316: a person with a good eye for judging things. Initial i, que is anticipated by f316’s catchword, not a new Japanese headword.
Meqiqiuo ſuru means exercising that discerning eye. The Portuguese begins the ability to see and judge, continued below.
Judging things well completes the appraisal example. The row is not an additional entry between Meqiqi and Meri.
Meri is harsh rebuke, paraphrased Nonoxiri with an abbreviated verbal ending. Scattered far-right ink marks do not form a secure word and are not invented as text.

runs.text: Fitono meri fifǒ ſuru coto nacare.

lines.note: The example prohibits rebuking or slandering others. Fifǒ has genuine f letters for h-row sounds, while ſuru starts with long ſ; Não begins the Portuguese prohibition.
The Portuguese completes the prohibition against rebuking and speaking ill of others. A word boundary is visible in mal dos; reprẽder retains its abbreviation.
Verbal Meri means rebuking or speaking ill of someone. The principal-form u stays abbreviated rather than being expanded in canonical text.
Nonoxiru supplies the verb’s Japanese synonym. The introductory punctuation is i, rather than i.; this synonym is not a Japanese word embedded in a Portuguese sentence.
This Meri is shrinking, diminishing, or sinking, paraphrased Feru. The printed dim- followed by nuirſe produces an unusual Portuguese spelling; no missing i is supplied from modern diminuir.
Nuirſe completes the divided Portuguese verb. Giga metta illustrates the ground sinking; Giga is preserved in its printed consonantal spelling.
The translation confirms that the ground sank. Metta fito then applies the shrinking image to an inhibited or bashful person, with Ho- continued below.

runs.text: mem acanhado, ou vergonhoſo q̃ com qualquer

lines.note: Mem completes Homem, describing a timid or bashful person. A faint initial c before om supports com rather than the draft’s om; this abraded letter remains a nonblocking reading caveat.

runs.text: palaura q̃ lhe dizem logo ſe encolhe, & acanha.

lines.note: Any word addressed to the person makes him shrink back and become embarrassed. This completes the figurative timid-person sense, not the literal ground-sinking example.
Merimecaxi, ſu, aita is making a cracking or crunching sound while eating. Its aita principal part is retained as historical morphology rather than modernized to a shita ending.
The alternative is making that sound by breaking hard things. This row completes the transitive sound-making definition before the corresponding intransitive form.
Merimeqi, u, eita describes hard things sounding or crackling. The principal form eita is visibly retained; the circumstances continue below.

runs.text: duras quando ſe comem, ou quebrão.

lines.note: The hard objects sound when eaten or broken. This completes the intransitive crunching or cracking definition.
This Merimeqi concerns making a clattering or creaking noise while moving. The printed principal form is eita, not OCR etta, and andã- continues below.
Do completes andando, with walking on boards as the example. The sound arises from movement over the boards rather than eating something hard.

runs.text: Modo de ſoar couſa que ſe quebra,

lines.note: Merimerito describes the sound of something breaking. The repeated meri sequence is meaningful sound symbolism, not an OCR duplication.
Ou parte adds splitting or breaking apart as an alternative. The short row completes the sound description before Mero.

Mero is a female servant, glossed Moça de ſeruiço. The supplied NINJAL index suggests Merǒ, but enlargement with extra top margin shows no secure accent over this copy’s o; Mero is retained without importing that mark. runs.text: O eſpertar, ou abrir os olhos do ſono.

lines.note: Meſamaxi is waking or opening one’s eyes from sleep. The source’s ſ spelling is preserved instead of imposing the spelling of a modern Japanese equivalent.
Meſamaxij and meſamaxij coto denote something new or extraordinary that arrests attention. No- begins the Portuguese noua across the row boundary.

runs.text: ua, ou extraordinaria a que hum aduirte, como

lines.note: Ua completes noua. The unusual thing attracts attention; enlargement resolves aduirte, including a dotted i omitted by OCR adurte. The historical spelling is retained rather than modernized.
The comparison is to waking in astonishment. This completes the striking-or-extraordinary sense of Meſamaxij rather than repeating only ordinary waking from sleep.
Meſare is described as an honorific verb. The abraded honrado remains supported by the visible letters and by the honorific uses enumerated below.
The verb is formed from Mexi, ſu, with formado rather than OCR farmado. This Japanese verb is explicitly mentioned inside a Portuguese grammatical explanation; ſignifi- continues below.

runs.text: ca tudo o que o verbo,

lines.note: Ca completes ſignifica; a visible space separates it from tudo. Xi, ſuru is the verb cited inside the Portuguese account of equivalent meanings, not a standalone example sentence.
The enumeration adds calling, boarding a vessel, and riding. Caual- continues below; these are alternative honorific uses of Meſare, not separate headwords.
Gar completes caualgar. Dressing is added, with Coſode- beginning an example of putting on a garment; the provisional st spelling in Vestirſe is retained.
Uo meſaruru completes the garment example. Item then adds eating and drinking; the visible comma after Item is retained and the Japanese example stays roman.

A visible pilcrow introduces Yadouo meſaruru, taking lodging. The damaged a and word spacing are recovered from compatible traces and the clear repeated yado example below; the OCR’s v douomeſaruru is not usable Japanese.
Gaſalharſe completes agaſalharſe, taking shelter. Fino curenu ſaqini yado begins the example about finding lodging before nightfall.
Uo meſareyo completes the polite instruction to take lodging. Yax. is an upright citation label, not part of the Japanese sentence; the Portuguese begins “before it becomes…”.
Noite completes the time condition. The imperative is visibly tomai, including final i omitted in the draft, followed by pouſada, lodging.
Meſarenaxi, ſu, aita describes bringing something about in this way. The heavily inked headword retains its legible sequence and historical aita principal part.

The example concerns conduct toward Nacaraidono. Although the Portuguese relation could suggest yeno, enlargement still supports the printed yono; it is retained, as is the weakly impressed mark in fǒy, rather than silently repaired from expected syntax.

The action causes a breach of the stated obligations. Meſarenaite is the historical -aite form corresponding to the printed principal part aita, not an omitted modern -shite sequence; Fazẽ continues below.

runs.text: do que faltaſte nos cõprimentos deuidos pera cõ

lines.note: Do completes Fazẽdo. The translation concerns failure in the courtesies or obligations owed toward the named person; cõprimentos has a damaged but compatible e and no extra tilde is supplied.

Nacaraidono completes the Portuguese phrase “toward Nacaraidono.” Although this entire short row is roman, the name functions inside a Portuguese explanation and is eligible for whole-word font review.
Met means destruction; Meſſuru illustrates being destroyed. Deſtruição has r rather than OCR e, and the final checked t of Met is not expanded.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de a cometer, ou

lines.note: Metametato describes a concerted or tumultuous attack. Its first t replaces OCR r and agrees with the repeated example below; the visible Portuguese a cometer spacing is retained.

runs.text: ſaltarem muitos com alguem em caſa pera o ma

lines.note: The explanation concerns many people attacking someone in a house in order to kill him. Ma continues as tar below without a visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: tar, ou derrubar, ou deſtruir algũa couſa,

lines.note: Tar completes matar. Derrubar has two printed r letters, not the draft’s one; knocking down or destroying something supplies the other applications of the adverb.
Metametato iyeye toricaqeta illustrates many people attacking the house. The repeated headword confirms the first t, and the attached iyeye spelling is preserved.

runs.text: Derão lhe na caſa muitos derepente.

lines.note: The Portuguese says many suddenly descended upon or attacked his house. Derepente remains printed as one word; the row completes the example above the bottom rule.

Metbǒ means destruction or perishing. The headword has b, not OCR h, matching the b in the same line’s Forobi; the subsequently consulted NINJAL headword also supports Metbǒ. The checked t is retained before b.
Metçuqe is a spy or observer. Metçuqeuo ſuru begins the example of acting as a spy, whose Portuguese translation starts on the following row.
Eſpiar completes the first example; Metçuqeuo yaru then means sending a spy. This is an indented continuation in the scan, so its placement is corrected under the same ID.
Eſpias completes Mandar eſpias. Metçuqeni mairu supplies coming as a spy; the printed continuation indentation is restored without merging the physical row.
Metdeqi is ending or being destroyed. The final upright S. is the written-usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese gloss.
Metdo is a Buddha’s death or passing, expressed by Fotoque inside the Portuguese explanation. The final Bup. identifies Buddhist terminology and remains upright.
Mete is the right hand, equated with Migui. Yũde begins the comparison with the bow hand or left side; the whole Japanese word is roman, including its nasal abbreviation.

Teni completes meteni; ainarabu means standing or being arranged alongside. The scan has n after ai, omitted in OCR aiarabu; the Portuguese describes equal placement of the two sides and retains the joined aparte.
Eſquerda and direita complete the comparison of equal placement on the left and right. These are the two sides mentioned by the preceding Japanese example.
Metgio means being destroyed or eliminated, paraphrased Mexxi nozoqu. The gloss continues with a second Portuguese participle; its provisional Estar typography is retained.
Desfeito completes the destruction or dissolution gloss. The short row is a continuation, not a separate headword or a fragment of Metgo below.
This Metgo denotes the time of death, paraphrased Meſſuru toqi. The pilcrow introduces the example on the next physical row.
Metgoni voyobu means reaching the hour of death, matching the Portuguese exactly. The initial vo of voyobu is preserved rather than modernized to o.
The second Metgo means after death or destruction, paraphrased Mexxite nochi. The printed Portuguese De pois remains separated; this homograph is not merged with the preceding time-of-death entry.
Ou deſtruição completes the alternative to death. The row closes the second Metgo entry before the stronger term for total destruction.
Metjin means destroying completely, first paraphrased Mexxi tçuquru. The visible i, introduces Cotogotocu, whose predicate is on the following row; its comma replaces the draft’s stop.
Meſſuru completes Cotogotocu meſſuru, total destruction. The Portuguese states that sense directly; the repeated long-s types are retained.
Metqiacu is equated with Mecqiacu, which the italic potius recommends in preference. The dotted i in potius replaces OCR t; Idem refers back to total destruction.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de olhar hum pera

lines.note: Metometo is an adverb describing people looking directly at one another. The reciprocal description continues on the next row.

runs.text: outro com os olhos fitos. Vt,

lines.note: The gaze is fixed on the other person. Vt introduces Metometo miauaſuru, with the verb placed on the following physical row.

runs.text: Olhar hum pera outro com os

lines.note: Miauaſuru completes the reciprocal-looking example. The Portuguese begins its translation as looking at one another with fixed eyes.

Olhos fitos completes the preceding example. At the far right, a parenthesis-like mark and caſar ſe complete Metori on the next row but are physically printed here. The chosen r is tightly compressed beside a and remains a minor reading uncertainty; the marriage gloss and surviving strokes support it. Both displaced segments remain in named far-right spans, not moved into the next row.

runs.text: O tomar o homem molher, ou

lines.note: Metori means a man taking a wife. The Portuguese ends in ou; its alternative caſar ſe is displaced to the far right of the preceding physical row, so no text is invented or duplicated here.
Metzai is the destruction or removal of sin, paraphrased Tçumiuo meſſuru. The Portuguese object continues as peccado below.
Peccado completes the removal-of-sin definition. Metzai xǒjenno cudocu begins an example connecting removal of sin and cultivation of good with religious merit.

runs.text: O Deſtruir o peccado, & obrar vir-

lines.note: Nari completes the Japanese statement. The Portuguese translates destroying sin and practising virtues; vir- is visibly divided at the right rule.
Tudes completes virtudes, and merecimẽto supplies merit. The nasal abbreviation is retained rather than expanded to a modern spelling.
This Mexi is cooked rice, directly glossed Arroz cozido. It is a separate noun from the following honorific verb and summons noun.
Mexi, ſu, exita has the meanings of Meſare, as the next row explains. The Portuguese noun is physically divided after ſignificaço-, preserving the printed historical vowel sequence.

The continuation is ẽs, with a visible e under the tilde, not OCR õs. Meſare, uru is a verb cited within Portuguese explanatory prose, and V.g. introduces the examples “call” and “eat,” rather than the OCR’s Vag.
Drinking and riding complete the list of meanings. Vide ſuprà directs the reader to the earlier Meſare entry; the whole apparatus remains italic.
This Mexi is a summons from a noble person. The scan has the joined Chamamento and two long-s letters in peſſoa, not Cha mamento or peſtoa; Me- begins the response-to-a-summons example.

runs.text: Ir, ou acodir a ochamado de

lines.note: Xini completes Mexini; vôzuru means responding to the summons. The Portuguese reads the joined acodir, with the damaged d supported by its remaining stem and the phrase, rather than OCR aco dir. The printed a ochamado spacing is retained.
Peßoa alta completes the summons as one from a person of high station. The distinctive ß-like type is retained rather than equated automatically with the two long-s types above.
Mexiague gives the verb for raising or causing something or someone to rise. Its abbreviated principal forms remain separated by the printed commas.

runs.text: ſubir a algum grao, dignidade, ou lugar mais

lines.note: The definition extends to raising someone to a grade, dignity, or higher position. Mais modifies alto on the following row, not a missing noun.
Alto completes the elevation gloss. Vatacuxino ſacazzuqiuo begins an example about the speaker’s drinking cup, with the object particle attached.
Mexi aguerareta completes the example of taking up the cup. The Portuguese begins Aleuantoume, ou to-, with tomoume divided across the line break.

runs.text: moume o Sacazzuqui que eu bebi. ¶

lines.note: Moume completes tomoume. Sacazzuqui names the drinking cup within the Portuguese explanation and is eligible for whole-word font review; Yacuuo then begins a separate example concerning an office.
Mexi aguru completes Yacuuo mexi aguru, explained as removing or depriving someone of office. This is another use of the compound, not the modern eating sense imposed on every occurrence.
Mexi agueraruru is additionally used of buying, in the honorific form. The Portuguese subject appears on the next physical row.
The buyer is an honoured or noble person. Peſſoa has two long-s types in the scan, not the draft’s one; the remaining spelling and tilde in algũa are retained.
Mexi atçume means assembling or summoning people. The damaged initial has the remaining strokes of M, not OCR N, and the example and regional variant below repeat the same mexi compound.

Te completes gente. The Portuguese identifies the usage in Cami and gives Mexiatçumeraruru across the break; Cami is an embedded Japanese regional name, while the cited verb is also part of this Portuguese metalinguistic statement.
Ruru completes the cited regional verb. It is used in speaking of a noble person; Vt then introduces a separate Japanese example beginning Nin, without a supplied line-end hyphen.

Juo continues Ninjuo, the people being assembled. The verb reads atçumeraruru, with m rather than OCR n; the damaged e retains compatible traces. The printed single-u boundary in Ninjuo is not silently expanded.
Juntar completes ajuntar. The Portuguese explains summoning or convening people, closing this entry above the separate bottom signature and catchword.
